Hello inla group,
Just a quick question about the ordering from function inla.finn. Assuming my structure matrix is R, then with inla.finn I get the ordering to reduce the matrix bandwidth. The samples that I get in m, is it based on R, or the permuted R?
m = inla.finn(R, reordering="band")

Many thanks,
Cici

messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inla.finn
parts:
The samples are based on R. The reordering is used internally to compute the sample, but it is returned in the natural order.

Best wishes

Dan

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inla.finn
parts:
Small clarifications:
inla.finn is an internal function that does whatever I needed at a particular point in time, which happened to be visualisation of the reorderings and calculating samples. Currently it is also used internally by inla.spde.sample, which is the function you should call if you want a sample, since inla.finn may change without warning. The function, inla.finn calls the inla program, which calculates a reordering as well as a sample (so it is not calculated in R), and the sample is returned in the same order as the original precision matrix.

Thanks for the additional note  - it is a rather important warning.

So my understanding is that the cholesky decomposition used in the function inla.finn is not applied on the rank deficiency matrix R directly. But rather,  first add a bit on the diagonal of R to make it non-singular,  then use the inla.finn function to generate samples from the GMRF.  This question draws to my attention when I start using R library spam recently. The function chol.spam seems to work fine with a rank deficient spatial adjacency matrix. But it gives error message about singularity when I tried a made-up rank deficient matrix. So, in Rue 2001 Fast sampling Gaussian Random field paper, the sampling algorithm for the GMRF is described to "first note that computing the Cholesky factorization of the band matrix Q with bandwidth b_w Q=LL^T is a standard problem in numerical linear algebra". Strictly speaking, the Q used in the formula is not the real precision matrix Q elsewhere in the paper. It is the new Q after applying the trick of adding some value to the diagonal.

Sorry this might be a dumb question but I am not a numerical linear algebra person. However, I do want to make sure I understand what the black box is doing.

Thank you very much,
Cici

messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: inla.finn
parts:
Hi Cici,

This is a rather complicated question!

To begin with, almost everything you could ever need to know on this
topic is in Nick Higham's excellent (if rather daunting) book
"Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (in particular the
chapter on Cholesky decompositions).

So lets start at the beginning: You probably shouldn't be computing
the Cholesky factorisation of a semi-definite matrix. While it's
"possible", it's very difficult for the obvious reason that Q+ E for
almost any E is no longer semidefinite, and so the operation is not
going to be stable in the presence of rounding error (even in the best
case, it can be catastrophically unstable).

More importantly, none of the operations make sense for sampling etc
for GMRFs unless L (and hence Q) is non-singular! Adding a small
diagonal will "fix" this, it's almost certainly not what you want to
do - you either want to add a "large" matrix in the form of
conditioning on data, or you want to condition on a system of linear
constraints (eg sum to zero constraints) that make the conditional
GMRF proper. Rue (2001) always assumes that Q is a proper precision
matrix (and hence SPD), similarly in the book whenever an intrinsic
field is used, it is sampled etc conditional on linear constraints.

To the best of my knowledge, which is incomplete here, INLA does not
(by default) add a small number to the diagonal for stability. (You
can make it do this with the "diagonal" option in control.inla, but,
as above, you shouldn't).

The correct behaviour when you have a positive semi-definite matrix is
for it to either compute a singular L [if you're a) lucky and b) using
pivoting)] or to fail because it encountered a zero (or negative)
pivot.

Now, let's talk about truth, computing, and numerical linear algebra!
For the Cholesky triangle L that the computer gives you LL^T is NEVER
equal to Q. Absolutely unequivocally never. The best that you can
ever say is that ||Q - LL^T|| is small (there are classical bounds on
this that say that ||Q - LL^T|| <= c_n u ||A||, where c_n is a small
constant and u~1e-16 is the machine precision. Note that this *does
not* say that the computed L is close to the true Cholesky factor of
Q. In practice, this doesn't matter - it's rare that real problems
are so catastrophically ill conditioned that you can compute an answer
and it's really really wrong.

In practice, if you have a poorly conditioned matrix (specifically if
20n^{3/2}||Q||||Q^{-1}||u >1), then the Cholesky decomposition is not
guaranteed to be computable in finite arithmetic. This is what
happens when the Cholesky factorisation fails (assuming Q is SPSD!).
There is pretty much nothing that you can do about this, other than
use higher precision floating point arithmetic, which most of the time
isn't practical! It's entirely possible that the semidefinite matrix
that you "made up" was too ill conditioned for chol.spam to be able to
compute anything with it.

I hope this helps.

Dan

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: inla.finn
parts: On Thu, 2012-02-16 at 09:51 +0200, Daniel Simpson wrote:

> To the best of my knowledge, which is incomplete here, INLA does not
> (by default) add a small number to the diagonal for stability. (You
> can make it do this with the "diagonal" option in control.inla, but,
> as above, you shouldn't).

confirmed.

a comment on the diagonal issue: if precision matrix Q is
singular/numerically singular, then adding a diagonal d to it

Q' = Q + diag(d)

and then producing samples from it, has a clear interpretation.

consider the following model

x ~ GMRF(Q)

with observations

y | x ~ N(x, diag(d))

that are all zero, so y=0. then x|y=0 has precision matrix Q' and mean
zero. so adding 'd' to the diagonal, just give you samples from x|y=0,
using the model above.

that's fine. If you're doing that in your acceptance probability, then
you will target the"wrong" distribution.

See haavard's response for the interpretation
